sections.name: Digital Sculpting Fundamentals (ZBrush & Blender)
sections.explanation_simple: Digital sculpting is like working with clay on your computer. Instead of pushing vertices one by one, you use brushes that push, pull, smooth, and carve the surface like real clay. ZBrush is the industry standard (used for every character in Marvel movies and AAA games). Blender has a powerful sculpting mode built in for free. The key difference from regular 3D modeling: sculpting works with millions of polygons (like high-detail clay), while regular modeling works with thousands (like Lego blocks). You sculpt the high detail first, then create a low-poly version for the game.
key_concepts: Dyntopo (Dynamic Topology): Automatically adds polygons where you need detail, removes where you don't
Multiresolution Modifier: Subdivides mesh evenly, keeps all levels of detail
Draw Brush: The main brush - pushes and pulls surface
Clay Brush: Adds volume like real clay building
Crease Brush: Makes sharp indentations (muscle lines, wrinkles)
Smooth Brush: Softens rough areas
Masking: Protecting areas from being affected by brushes
Symmetry: Mirroring your strokes across X, Y, or Z axis
Alphas: Greyscale images used as brush stamps (add skin texture, scales, etc.)
Reference: NEVER sculpt without reference images (anatomy books, photos, etc.)
Primary Forms: Big shapes (head shape, torso volume)
Secondary Forms: Medium details (muscles, fat pads)
Tertiary Details: Small details (pores, wrinkles, skin folds)
sections.learning_path: Understanding 3D clay -> Basic brushes (draw, clay, smooth, crease) -> Dyntopo vs Multires -> Primary forms (blocking out) -> Anatomy basics -> Secondary forms (muscles) -> Tertiary details (skin, wrinkles) -> Alphas and custom brushes -> Stylized vs realistic sculpting -> Posing the sculpt

sections.name: ZBrush Mastery
sections.explanation_simple: ZBrush is the most powerful digital sculpting tool in the world. It can handle 100+ million polygon meshes in real-time, which is insane for a single computer. Every major film and game character is sculpted in ZBrush. The interface is unique (not like other 3D software) and takes getting used to, but once you learn it, you can create incredibly detailed characters, creatures, and environments. ZBrush uses 'Pixols' (pixel + polygon hybrid) instead of traditional meshes, which is why it can handle such high detail.
key_concepts: Pixol: ZBrush's unique pixel+polygon hybrid technology
3D Gizmo: Transform, scale, rotate objects (like G in Blender)
Subtools: Each object (armor, body, weapon) is a separate subtool in one ZBrush project
ZRemesher: Auto-retopology tool that creates clean quad meshes from sculpts
Project All: Projects high-poly detail onto a new retopologized mesh
UV Master: Automatic UV unwrapping (good enough for most game assets)
Polypaint: Painting directly on the surface without needing UVs
Morph Target: Saves a 'snapshot' of mesh state for blending
Transpose: ZBrush's posing system (rotate parts of your sculpt like a puppet)
GoZ: One-click transfer between ZBrush and other software (Maya, Blender, UE5)
DynaMesh: Evenly redistributes polygons for cleaner sculpting
MicroMesh: Places millions of small objects (scales, tiles, feathers) on surface
FiberMesh: Generates realistic hair, fur, grass directly in ZBrush
NoiseMaker: Adds procedural surface detail (armor scratches, skin texture)
Decimation Master: Reduces polygon count while preserving detail

code_examples.title: ZBrush Workflow: Blockout to Final
code_examples.code:
# ===== COMPLETE ZBRUSH CHARACTER WORKFLOW =====

"""
PHASE 1: BLOCKOUT (Primary Forms)
  1. Start with ZSphere or Sphere3D
  2. Use Move brush to shape basic silhouette
  3. ClayBuildup brush to add volume to body parts
  4. Split into Subtools (Head, Torso, Arms, Legs)
  5. Use Transpose Master to pose after blocking

PHASE 2: DETAILING (Secondary Forms)
  1. Divide mesh to higher resolution (Ctrl+D)
  2. Standard brush for muscle definition
  3. DamStandard brush for sharp creases (muscle separations)
  4. Clay brush for building up forms
  5. hPolish brush for flattening areas (bone landmarks)

PHASE 3: SURFACE DETAILS (Tertiary Forms)
  1. Alpha brushes for skin pores, wrinkles
  2. NoiseMaker for surface texture
  3. Layer brush for subtle skin folds
  4. Make sure subdivision levels are 6-7 for detail

PHASE 4: RETOPOLOGY & BAKE
  1. ZRemesher with proper target poly count
  2. Create UVs with UV Master
  3. Project All to transfer detail
  4. Export as GoZ to Maya/Blender for rigging
  5. Bake maps (Normal, AO, Cavity) from high to low poly
"""

# ===== ZBRUSH SHORTCUTS =====
/*
  B - Brush menu
  I - RGB intensity
  Shift+F - Wireframe overlay
  Ctrl+D - Divide (increase subdivisions)
  Shift+D - Lower subdivision level
  D - Higher subdivision level
  Ctrl+Z - Undo (ZBrush has unlimited undo!)
  Alt - Invert brush effect (hold while brushing)
  Space - Quick menu
  X - Toggle symmetry
  Shift+Click on canvas - Rectangular zoom
  Ctrl+Shift+Drag - Hide masked area
  Ctrl+Click on empty canvas - Show all
*/

sections.learning_path: ZBrush interface basics -> ZSpheres -> Blockout sculpting -> Subtools management -> Subdivision levels -> Refining anatomy -> Brush mastery (Standard, Clay, DamStandard) -> Alphas for detail -> Retopology with ZRemesher -> UV Master -> Polypaint -> FiberMesh for hair -> MicroMesh for scales/armor -> Decimation for game export

sections.name: PBR Texturing with Substance Painter & Designer
sections.explanation_simple: PBR (Physically Based Rendering) texturing is how you make 3D models look real. Instead of just painting a flat color on a model, you create multiple maps that describe how light interacts with the surface: Albedo (base color), Roughness (how smooth/shiny), Metalness (is it metal?), Normal (fake surface bumps), and AO (ambient shadows in crevices). Substance Painter is like Photoshop for 3D models - you paint directly on the model and it creates all these maps automatically. Substance Designer lets you create procedural materials (brick, wood, metal) using node graphs.
key_concepts: Albedo Map: Base color of the surface (no lighting or shadows)
Roughness Map: How rough (0 = mirror smooth, 1 = completely rough/diffuse)
Metalness Map: Is this area metal? (1 = metal, 0 = non-metal, no in-between)
Normal Map: Fakes 3D detail by modifying how light bounces off surface
Ambient Occlusion (AO): Shadows in crevices and corners
Height/Displacement Map: Actually moves vertices for real 3D depth (expensive)
Emissive Map: Areas that glow (neon signs, eyes, screens)
Opacity Map: Transparency (glass, leaves, cloth)
Smart Materials: Substance Painter materials that auto-detect surface features
Smart Masks: Auto-masks for edge wear, dirt, scratches based on mesh curvature
UDIM: Multiple UV tiles for very high resolution texturing (film/VFX)
UDK: Channel packing (combining maps into one texture)
Texel Density: How many pixels per meter of 3D surface (consistency is key)
Trimming: Creating reusable texture sheets for modular environments
Procedural vs Hand-painted: CAD-designed patterns vs artistic textures

code_examples.title: Substance Painter: Smart Material Creation
code_examples.code:
# ===== SUBSTANCE PAINTER SMART MATERIAL WORKFLOW =====

"""
CREATING A WEATHERED METAL SMART MATERIAL:

LAYER 1: BASE METAL
  - Color: Dark gray (RGB 80,80,80)
  - Metalness: 1.0
  - Roughness: 0.3
  - Height: 0

LAYER 2: PAINT COATING
  - Color: Red (RGB 180,40,30)
  - Metalness: 0.0
  - Roughness: 0.6
  - Height: 0.01
  - Mask: "Grunge Map" blended with "Position" (top areas stay painted)

LAYER 3: EDGE WEAR
  - Metalness: 1.0
  - Roughness: 0.2
  - Mask: "Curvature" (edges only) + "Grunge" for random variation
  - Effect: Reveals the bare metal under the paint

LAYER 4: DIRT/DUST
  - Color: Brownish (RGB 120,100,80)
  - Roughness: 0.9
  - Metalness: 0.0
  - Mask: "Ambient Occlusion" (dirt in crevices) + "Position" (dirt at bottom)

LAYER 5: SCRATCHES
  - Mask: "Scratches" generator with random direction
  - Effect: Thin bright metallic lines

OUTPUT SETTINGS (for Unreal Engine 5):
  - Albedo (RGB) @ 2K (2048x2048)
  - Normal (RG) @ 2K (BC5 compression)
  - Roughness (R) + Metalness (G) + AO (B) packed into one texture
  - Emissive (if needed) @ 2K
"""

# ===== SUBSTANCE DESIGNER: PROCEDURAL BRICK WALL =====
"""
NODE GRAPH:

1. Tile Generator (Bricks pattern)
   |
2. -+-> Slope Blur (weathered edges on bricks)
   |
3. -+-> Non-Uniform Blur + Quantize (deformed bricks, random variation)
   |
4. -+-> Histogram Scan + Levels (adjust contrast of mortar)
   |
5. -+-> Ambient Occlusion (compute AO from height map)
   |
6. -+-> Height Blend (combine with dirt/grunge texture)
   |
7. OUTPUT:
   - Height Map (for Normal calculation and Displacement)
   - Base Color (albedo of bricks + mortar)
   - Normal Map (computed from Height)
   - AO Map
   - Roughness (rougher mortar, smoother bricks)
"""

// Substance Designer - Custom Pixel Processor node
// HLSL code for tile blending:
float2 Random(float2 uv)
{
    uv = frac(uv * float2(123.34, 456.21));
    uv += dot(uv, uv + 19.17);
    return frac(uv * float2(78.92, 45.63));
}

// Slightly randomize each brick's color for realism
float4 Process(float4 color1, float4 color2, float2 uv)
{
    float2 tilePos = floor(uv * float2(4, 8)); // 4 columns, 8 rows
    float2 rand = Random(tilePos);
    
    // Slightly vary each brick's color and roughness
    float3 brickColor = color1.rgb + (rand.x - 0.5) * 0.1;
    float roughness = color1.a + (rand.y - 0.5) * 0.2;
    
    return float4(brickColor, roughness);
}

sections.learning_path: PBR theory (Albedo, Roughness, Metalness, Normal, AO) -> Substance Painter basics -> Smart materials -> Masking (curvature, position, AO) -> Weathering and wear -> Texture optimization -> Substance Designer fundamentals -> Node graphs -> Material functions -> Export to game engine

sections.name: Character & Creature Rigging
sections.explanation_simple: Rigging is creating a digital skeleton for a 3D model so it can be animated. Think of it like a puppet: you build the armature (bones), attach the mesh (weight painting), and create controls so animators can easily pose it. A good rig gives the animator total control while being easy to use. Bad rigs make animation a nightmare. Professional rigs include IK/FK switching (using controllers on the hands and feet vs natural arm movement), stretchy limbs (for cartoon characters), facial controls (every subtle expression), and secondary animation (jiggling fat, floppy ears).
key_concepts: Armature: The skeleton structure made of bones
Bone: A single joint in the skeleton (has head and tail position)
Joint: The pivot point of a bone
Hierarchy: Parent-child relationships (root -> spine -> chest -> shoulder -> arm -> hand)
IK (Inverse Kinematics): Hand stays in place, arm bends naturally (used for feet on ground, hands on objects)
FK (Forward Kinematics): Rotate each bone from parent to child (used for arms swinging naturally)
IK/FK Switch: A rig that can swap between IK and FK modes (standard in all pro rigs)
Weight Painting: How much each bone influences each vertex (painted with gradients)
Vertex Groups: Blender's way of storing bone weights per vertex
Deformation: How the mesh moves when bones move
Constraints: Rules that limit bone movement (e.g., knee can't bend backward)
Control Bones: Extra bones that animators use (not part of the skeleton, just controllers)
Shape Keys (Morph Targets): Pre-made mesh deformations for facial expressions
Drivers: Automatically control one property based on another (bone rotation drives shape key value)
Auto-Rigging: Tools that create rigs automatically (Rigify in Blender, AccuRig, etc.)

code_examples.title: Complete Rigify Rig Pipeline (Blender Python)
code_examples.code:
# ===== BLENDER PYTHON: METARIG SETUP =====
import bpy

def setup_character_rig(character_name="Character"):
    """
    Creates a complete rig for a character using Rigify.
    """
    # Select the character mesh
    mesh = bpy.context.active_object
    if not mesh or mesh.type != 'MESH':
        print("Please select a mesh first")
        return

    # Add Rigify metarig
    bpy.ops.object.armature_human_metarig_add()
    metarig = bpy.context.active_object
    metarig.name = f"{character_name}_Metarig"

    # Scale metarig to match character
    # (You'd do this manually in the viewport)

    # Generate the actual rig
    bpy.ops.object.select_all(action='DESELECT')
    metarig.select_set(True)
    bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = metarig
    bpy.ops.pose.rigify_generate()

    # The generated rig is now active
    rig = bpy.context.active_object
    rig.name = f"{character_name}_Rig"

    # Parent mesh to rig with automatic weights
    bpy.ops.object.select_all(action='DESELECT')
    mesh.select_set(True)
    rig.select_set(True)
    bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = rig
    bpy.ops.object.parent_set(type='ARMATURE_AUTO')

    print(f"Rig created for {character_name}")
    print("Controls:")
    print("  - Select the rig and go to Pose Mode")
    print("  - Select the control circles (green, blue, etc.) to pose")
    print("  - Use the Properties panel for IK/FK switching")

# Run it:
# setup_character_rig("MyHero")

# ===== MANUAL RIG: IK/FK System =====
import bpy

def create_ik_fk_arm(name="Arm"):
    """Create an arm rig with IK/FK switching."""
    bpy.ops.object.armature_add()
    armature = bpy.context.active_object
    armature.name = f"{name}_Rig"

    # Enter edit mode to build bones
    bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='EDIT')
    edit_bones = armature.data.edit_bones

    # Create FK chain
    upper_arm = edit_bones.new(f"{name}_FK_Upper")
    upper_arm.head = (0, 0, 1)  # Shoulder
    upper_arm.tail = (0, 0, 0.5)  # Elbow

    forearm = edit_bones.new(f"{name}_FK_Forearm")
    forearm.parent = upper_arm
    forearm.head = upper_arm.tail
    forearm.tail = (0, 0, 0)  # Wrist

    # Create IK bone (same positions, different parenting)
    ik_target = edit_bones.new(f"{name}_IK_Target")
    ik_target.head = (0, 0, 0)  # Wrist
    ik_target.tail = (0, 0, -0.3)  # Below wrist

    # Pole target for IK (controls elbow direction)
    pole = edit_bones.new(f"{name}_Pole")
    pole.head = (-0.3, 0, 0.5)  # Behind elbow
    pole.tail = (-0.4, 0, 0.5)

    # Switch to pose mode to add constraints
    bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='OBJECT')
    bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='POSE')
    pose_bones = armature.pose.bones

    # Add IK constraint to forearm
    ik_constraint = pose_bones[forearm.name].constraints.new('IK')
    ik_constraint.target = armature
    ik_constraint.subtarget = ik_target.name
    ik_constraint.pole_target = armature
    ik_constraint.pole_subtarget = pole.name
    ik_constraint.pole_angle = 0
    ik_constraint.chain_count = 2

    # Add custom bone shapes (circles for controls)
    # ... (would need to create widget objects)

    print(f"IK/FK arm rig created for {name}")

# Run it:
# create_ik_fk_arm("Left")

code_examples.title: Facial Rigging with Shape Keys (Blender)
code_examples.code:
# ===== BLENDER PYTHON: FACIAL SHAPE KEY SYSTEM =====
import bpy

def create_facial_shape_keys(mesh_name="Character_Head"):
    """Create a complete set of facial shape keys."""

    mesh = bpy.data.objects.get(mesh_name)
    if not mesh or mesh.type != 'MESH':
        print(f"Mesh '{mesh_name}' not found")
        return

    # Select the mesh
    bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = mesh
    mesh.select_set(True)

    # Enter edit mode to create shape keys
    # First, add the Basis (base shape)
    basis_key = mesh.data.shape_keys.key_blocks.get("Basis")
    if not basis_key:
        mesh.shape_key_add(name="Basis", from_mix=False)

    # Define all the shape keys we need
    shape_keys = [
        # Brows
        "Brow_Raise_Left", "Brow_Raise_Right", "Brow_Lower_Left", "Brow_Lower_Right",
        # Eyes
        "Eye_Blink_Left", "Eye_Blink_Right", "Eye_Wide_Left", "Eye_Wide_Right",
        "Eye_Squint_Left", "Eye_Squint_Right", "Eye_Look_Up", "Eye_Look_Down",
        "Eye_Look_Left", "Eye_Look_Right",
        # Mouth
        "Mouth_Smile", "Mouth_Frown", "Mouth_Open", "Mouth_Ooh",
        "Mouth_Pucker", "Mouth_Stretch", "Mouth_Dimpler",
        "Lip_Raise_Upper", "Lip_Raise_Lower", "Lip_Corner_Puller",
        # Jaw
        "Jaw_Open", "Jaw_Left", "Jaw_Right", "Jaw_Forward",
        # Cheeks
        "Cheek_Suck", "Cheek_Puff", "Cheek_Raise",
        # Nose
        "Nose_Wrinkle", "Nose_Flare",
        # Tongue
        "Tongue_Out", "Tongue_Up",
        # Additional
        "Head_Tilt", "Neck_Flex",
    ]

    for name in shape_keys:
        key = mesh.shape_key_add(name=name, from_mix=True)
        # Set value to 0 (it's created at 1.0 by default from_mix)
        key.value = 0.0

    print(f"Created {len(shape_keys)} facial shape keys on {mesh_name}")

# The actual vertex positions would need to be edited manually
# in Edit Mode with the shape key selected.
# This function creates all the keys so you can edit them.

# ===== DRIVEN FACIAL CONTROLS =====
# Create a bone that drives shape keys

def create_facial_bone_drivers(rig_name="Head_Rig", mesh_name="Character_Head"):
    """Link facial bones to shape key values."""

    rig = bpy.data.objects.get(rig_name)
    mesh = bpy.data.objects.get(mesh_name)

    if not rig or not mesh:
        print("Rig or mesh not found")
        return

    # Example: Mouth_Open bone drives Jaw_Open shape key
    mouth_bone = rig.pose.bones.get("Mouth_Open_Bone")
    if mouth_bone and mesh.data.shape_keys:
        shape_key = mesh.data.shape_keys.key_blocks.get("Jaw_Open")
        if shape_key:
            # Create a driver
            driver = shape_key.driver_add("value")
            driver.driver.type = 'AVERAGE'

            # Add variable: bone rotation
            var = driver.driver.variables.new()
            var.name = "mouth_rot"
            var.type = 'TRANSFORMS'

            # Target: the bone
            target = var.targets[0]
            target.id = rig
            target.bone_target = mouth_bone.name
            target.transform_type = 'ROT_Y'
            target.transform_space = 'LOCAL_SPACE'

            # Expression: simple mapping
            driver.driver.expression = "mouth_rot"

    print("Facial drivers created")

# Run:
# create_facial_shape_keys("MyCharacter")
# create_facial_bone_drivers("Head_Rig", "MyCharacter")

sections.learning_path: Armature basics (bones, hierarchy) -> Parenting bones -> Weight painting fundamentals -> FK rigging -> IK rigging -> IK/FK switching -> Custom bone shapes (controls) -> Constraints (limit rotation, copy transform) -> Facial shape keys -> Drivers for facial controls -> Auto-rigging tools (Rigify) -> Quadruped rigs -> Advanced deformation (muscle systems, jiggle bones)
